1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SCT: Schema Conversion Tool; DMS: Database Migration Service; ML: machine learning; PK: partition key; SK: sort key; LF: Lake Formation; ORC: Optimized Row Columnar; MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; CDC: change data capture; RDS: Relational Database Service; DAX: DynamoDB Accelerator; EBS: Elastic Block Store; TTL: time to live

  • Design schemas for Amazon Redshift, DynamoDB and Lake Formation
  • Handle changes to the characteristics of data (schema evolution)
  • Perform schema conversion with AWS SCT and AWS DMS Schema Conversion
  • Establish data lineage with SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking and SageMaker Catalog
  • Describe indexing, partitioning, compression and other optimization practices
  • Describe vectorization and how a Bedrock knowledge base uses it

2Designing Schemas (skill 2.4.1)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Models Its Data

  • The warehouse needs fast reports by customer, route and month
  • The tracking app must fetch a shipment and its latest events by ID
  • The lake holds telemetry by day, and analysts want one governed table
  • Your job: design each schema around how the data will be read

Amazon Redshift: dimensional design

  • Star schema: a fact table (measures such as weight, cost, delay; foreign keys) joined to dimension tables (descriptive attributes). Snowflake schema normalizes dimensions further (more joins)
  • Choose keys for joins and filters:
    • Distribution key (KEY style) on the column used to join the large fact table to a large dimension: co-locates rows and avoids shuffles
    • ALL style for small, slowly changing dimensions; EVEN when there is no clear join key; AUTO lets Redshift decide
    • Sort key on the column most used in range filters (usually date) so blocks can be skipped
    • Column compression encoding (AUTO by default) reduces storage and I/O
  • Primary and foreign key constraints are informational in Redshift: the optimizer uses them, but Redshift does not enforce them
  • Denormalize for read speed when updates are rare

Amazon DynamoDB: design from the access patterns

  • List every access pattern first (get a shipment, list a truck's events by time); design keys to serve them, not the entities
  • Partition key: many distinct values, evenly used (shipment ID); sort key orders items within a partition and allows range queries (begins_with, between)
  • Single-table design: several entity types in one table with generic keys (PK, SK), so one query returns related items
  • Secondary indexes: GSI (different partition and sort key; own capacity; eventually consistent; add or remove any time), LSI (same partition key, different sort key; created with the table; shares capacity; strong consistency option)
  • Limits: an item is at most 400 KB; no joins, so model relationships by key design or duplicate data
  • Attribute values can be strings, numbers, binary, sets, lists and maps; the table is schemaless apart from the key

AWS Lake Formation: lake tables

  • Lake Formation governs databases and tables in the Glue Data Catalog over S3: design table schemas with column names and types, partition keys (such as date), file format (Parquet) and location
  • Add security design: LF-tags (attribute-based) and column, row and cell filters (Module 15)
  • Separate zones: raw (landing), curated (clean, typed), consumption (aggregated), with catalog databases per zone
Exam tip

"Large fact table joined to a large dimension on customer_id" → KEY distribution on customer_id for both. "Queries filter by date ranges" → sort key on the date column. "DynamoDB table needs a second way to query" → a global secondary index.

3Schema Evolution and Changing Data (skill 2.4.2)

  • Schema evolution = the structure of data changes over time: new columns, removed columns, renamed or retyped fields, new partitions, new sources
  • Principles: additive changes are safest (add optional fields with defaults); avoid renaming and changing types in place; version schemas; test before release
Layer How it handles change
Formats Avro, Parquet, ORC and JSON carry or tolerate added columns; CSV is positional and breaks easily; Iceberg supports add, drop, rename and reorder columns and partition evolution without rewriting data
Glue Schema Registry Central, versioned schemas (Avro, JSON Schema, Protobuf) for Kafka, MSK, Kinesis, Flink and Lambda; compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, the _ALL variants, NONE, DISABLED) reject unsafe versions; the registry is serverless and free
Glue crawlers Choose update behavior (update the table or ignore) and delete behavior when schemas drift
Glue jobs DynamicFrames tolerate mixed types (ResolveChoice); handle new columns explicitly
Redshift ALTER TABLE ADD/DROP COLUMN; some type changes (for example widening VARCHAR) are in place; others need a deep copy
DynamoDB Schemaless: new attributes need no migration; changing keys needs a new table or index
Athena / Glue tables Add columns at the end; schema-on-read exposes new fields
  • Backward compatible: new consumers can read old data; forward compatible: old consumers can read new data; full: both
  • Other changes to data characteristics: volume, velocity and quality shift: repartition, resize, re-index, add validation (Module 13)
Exam tip

"Producers add fields to events and consumers must not break" → AWS Glue Schema Registry with BACKWARD (or FULL) compatibility. "Table must add, rename and drop columns on a data lake without rewriting files" → Apache Iceberg.

4Schema Conversion (skill 2.4.3)

  • Schema conversion translates tables, views, indexes, procedures and functions from a source database engine to a different target engine (for example Oracle or SQL Server → PostgreSQL or Aurora), usually the first step of a heterogeneous migration
  • AWS DMS Schema Conversion: a managed feature in the DMS console: it assesses how much converts automatically, converts the schema and code, and lets you apply it to the target
  • AWS SCT (Schema Conversion Tool): the desktop application that does the same and produces an assessment report; code that cannot be converted is flagged for manual work [AWS SCT was removed from the exam's in-scope service list but the skill still names it]
  • Order: assess → convert schema → apply to target → migrate data with AWS DMS (full load and CDC)
  • Homogeneous migrations (same engine) need no conversion: use native tools or DMS
Exam tip

"Migrate an Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL" → convert the schema (DMS Schema Conversion or SCT), then move the data with DMS.

5Data Lineage (skill 2.4.4)

  • Data lineage records where data came from, what happened to it, and where it went: sources → transformations → outputs
  • Why: trust and debugging ("why is this number wrong?"), impact analysis (what breaks if this table changes), audits and compliance (prove the origin), reproducibility
  • AWS tools:
    • Amazon SageMaker Catalog captures and shows lineage across assets in SageMaker Unified Studio, so people can trace a dataset to its sources and consumers
    • Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking records the steps and artifacts of ML workflows (data sets, training jobs, models, endpoints) so a model can be traced to its training data
  • Capture options: job and pipeline logs, catalog metadata, and naming and tagging standards; combine with CloudTrail (who did it) and AWS Config (what changed)
Exam tip

"Show which source datasets and jobs produced a report" → lineage in SageMaker Catalog. "Trace a model back to the data and job that trained it" → SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.

6Indexing, Partitioning, Compression and Optimization (skill 2.4.5)

Technique What it does Where
Indexing A lookup structure that avoids scanning everything RDS/Aurora B-tree indexes; DynamoDB GSI/LSI; Redshift sort keys and zone maps; OpenSearch inverted and vector indexes
Partitioning Splits data by key so queries read only needed parts S3 prefixes (year=/month=) with Athena, Glue, Redshift Spectrum; DynamoDB partitions by partition key; Kinesis shards, Kafka partitions
Compression Smaller files, less I/O Parquet/ORC with Snappy or ZSTD; Redshift column encodings; gzip for text
Columnar formats Read only needed columns Parquet, ORC (Module 3)
File sizing Fewer, larger files (about 128 MB to 1 GB) Compaction jobs, Iceberg maintenance
Bucketing / clustering Group related rows in files Athena and Hive bucketing; Redshift sort and distribution
Denormalization and aggregation Precompute joins and rollups Materialized views, aggregate tables
Caching Keep hot results close DAX, MemoryDB, query result caching
  • Partition design rules: pick keys that queries filter on (usually date), with moderate cardinality; too many tiny partitions hurt, too few huge ones scan too much; keep layouts consistent
  • Trade-off: every index or copy speeds reads but costs writes and storage
Exam tip

"Athena scans too much data" → partition by the filter column, use Parquet, compress and compact files.

7Vectorization Concepts (skill 2.4.6)

  • Vectorization converts text, images or other data into vectors (embeddings) with an embedding model; similar meaning → nearby vectors
  • A knowledge base for Amazon Bedrock automates the pipeline for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG):
    1. Ingest documents from a data source (for example S3)
    2. Split into chunks (a chunking strategy)
    3. Embed each chunk with an embedding model
    4. Store vectors and the link to the source in a vector index (OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, and other supported vector stores)
    5. Sync when documents change (re-ingest)
    6. At query time: embed the question, retrieve the most similar chunks, add them to the prompt, and let the model answer
  • Choices: chunk size (too small loses context, too large dilutes meaning), embedding dimension (matches the model, for example 1,024 for several models), float or binary vectors (binary uses 1 bit per dimension: cheaper, less precise), metadata filters
  • RAG adds private knowledge without retraining the model
  • The vector store is a data store like any other: it needs access control, encryption, refresh and monitoring
Exam tip

"Give a foundation model access to private documents without retraining it" → RAG with a Bedrock knowledge base and a vector store.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1A Redshift fact table with billions of rows is joined constantly to a large customer dimension on customer_id, and queries are slow because of data movement. What should the engineer change?

  • AUse DISTSTYLE KEY on customer_id for both tables
  • BUse DISTSTYLE ALL on the fact table with billions of rows
  • CRemove the sort key from both tables
  • DMove the customer dimension to DynamoDB tables
Show the answer

Answer: A. KEY distribution on the join column co-locates matching rows on the same slices and avoids shuffling large tables. ALL on a huge table multiplies storage.

S2A DynamoDB table is keyed by shipment ID, and a new requirement is to list all shipments for a given customer sorted by date. What is the best solution?

  • AScan the whole table and filter the items by customer
  • BCreate a local secondary index after the table already exists
  • CCreate a global secondary index with customer ID as partition key and date as sort key
  • DMove the data to Amazon RDS and add a foreign key
Show the answer

Answer: C. A GSI provides a new key schema for the new query and can be added at any time. A scan is inefficient, and LSIs can only be created with the table.

S3Event producers occasionally add optional fields to Kafka messages, and existing consumers must keep working. Which approach enforces safe schema changes?

  • AA larger Amazon MSK cluster with more brokers and more partitions per topic
  • BConverting every message to CSV before it is published
  • CAWS Glue Schema Registry with BACKWARD or FULL compatibility
  • DDisabling schema checks on the consumers' side
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Schema Registry versions schemas and rejects new versions that violate the chosen compatibility mode, protecting consumers.

S4A company migrates an Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. In what order should the work be done?

  • AMigrate the data with DMS first and convert the schema afterwards
  • BConvert only the data and let the target create the tables itself
  • CConvert the schema with DMS Schema Conversion or SCT, apply it, then migrate the data with DMS
  • DCopy the Oracle files to S3 and query them from the new database
Show the answer

Answer: C. A heterogeneous migration converts the schema and code first, applies it to the target, and then moves data with DMS full load and change data capture.

S5A data lake in S3 needs to add, rename and drop columns over time without rewriting existing files, and support time travel. Which approach fits?

  • ACSV files with a header row
  • BGzip-compressed JSON
  • CApache Iceberg tables
  • DAmazon EBS volumes
Show the answer

Answer: C. Iceberg supports schema and partition evolution through table metadata and keeps snapshots for time travel.

S6Which TWO statements about a Bedrock knowledge base are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • AEmbeddings must be stored as plain text
  • BAt query time the question is embedded and the most similar chunks are added to the prompt
  • CThe foundation model is retrained every time a document is added
  • DDocuments are split into chunks and converted into embeddings stored in a vector index
  • EVectors can only be stored in Amazon S3 Glacier
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. The ingestion pipeline chunks and embeds documents, and retrieval embeds the question and adds similar chunks to the prompt. The model is not retrained.

S7An auditor asks which source tables and jobs produced a figure in a report. Which capability answers this?

  • AData lineage
  • BS3 versioning
  • CDynamoDB TTL
  • DRedshift sort keys
Show the answer

Answer: A. Lineage records where data came from and how it was transformed; SageMaker Catalog provides lineage for assets, and ML Lineage Tracking covers ML workflows.

S8Athena queries on a large dataset scan far more data than needed. Which TWO changes reduce the data scanned? (Select TWO.)

  • ADisable the AWS Glue Data Catalog
  • BPartition the data by the column queries filter on
  • CStore it as one large uncompressed CSV file
  • DStore the data as Parquet
  • EIncrease the Athena result retention
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Partitioning lets Athena skip folders and columnar Parquet lets it read only needed columns.

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Redshift schema Star schema; KEY dist on the join column, ALL small dims, EVEN/AUTO; sort key on date; constraints are informational
DynamoDB schema Access patterns first; high-cardinality partition key + sort key; single-table design; GSI (any time) vs LSI (at creation); 400 KB items
Lake Formation Catalog tables with types, partitions, Parquet, location; raw / curated / consumption zones; LF-tags
Schema evolution Additive and optional changes; Avro/Parquet/Iceberg; Glue Schema Registry compatibility (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, _ALL, NONE, DISABLED); crawler update behavior
Schema conversion DMS Schema Conversion (managed) and SCT (desktop): assess → convert → apply → DMS data; heterogeneous only
Lineage Source → transform → output; SageMaker Catalog (assets) and ML Lineage Tracking (ML)
Optimization Index, partition, compress, columnar, 128 MB–1 GB files, materialized views, cache; every index costs writes
Vectorization Chunk → embed → vector index → retrieve → augment prompt (RAG); float32 vs binary; Bedrock knowledge bases automate it
